```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.6, dpi = 90)
library(varm)
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(1)
```

`varm` estimates reduced-form and structural VARs, Bayesian VARs (Minnesota,
sum-of-coefficients, hierarchical, stochastic volatility, shrinkage priors),
time-varying-parameter VARs and local projections, with a compiled
(RcppArmadillo) engine. This tour takes about ten minutes and follows the
workflow of a typical applied project:

1. data, 2. lag choice, 3. estimation, 4. stability, 5. impulse responses with
bands, 6. variance decomposition, 7. historical decomposition, 8. forecasts,
9. a Bayesian VAR in three lines, 10. a local projection in three lines,
11. the tidy workflow: tibbles into `ggplot2`.

The API follows tidy-tools conventions. Variables are selected with tidyselect
(`vars = c(infl, rate)`, `shocks = rate`), results convert to tibbles with
`tidy()`, `glance()` and `augment()`, and every result has an `autoplot()` method
that returns an ordinary `ggplot2` object you can extend with `+ labs()`,
`+ theme_varm()` or any other layer.

Every object returned by `irf()`, `fevd()`, `hd()` and `forecast()` is built from
the same currency, a set of reduced-form parameter draws (`draws()`), so the
frequentist (bootstrap) and Bayesian code paths share one interface.

## 1. Data

`yraw` holds three quarterly US series from the Koop-Korobilis data set (1953Q1
to 2006Q3): inflation (`infl`), the unemployment rate (`unemp`) and a short-term
interest rate (`rate`). We add a `Date` column. `varm()` drops non-numeric columns
from the estimation but keeps a `Date` column as the time axis of the plots.

```{r data}
y <- yraw
y$date <- seq(as.Date("1953-01-01"), by = "quarter", length.out = nrow(y))
dim(yraw)
long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("infl", "unemp", "rate"), function(v) {
  data.frame(date = y$date, variable = v, value = y[[v]])
}))
ggplot(long, aes(date, value)) +
  geom_line(colour = varm_palette(1)) +
  facet_wrap(vars(variable), scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_varm()
```

`varm()` accepts a data frame (preferred), a matrix or a `ts`. Use `vars =` to pick
the endogenous variables with tidyselect, for example
`varm(y, p = 2, vars = c(infl, rate))` for a bivariate system. All three series
are persistent levels; we keep them in levels, which is standard for a VAR used for
dynamics and forecasting (see `vignette("var-theory")`, "Reduced-form VAR: theory,
inference and use", for when this is and is not appropriate).

## 2. Lag choice

`var_select()` evaluates AIC, Hannan-Quinn (HQ), Schwarz (SC) and the (log) final
prediction error (FPE) for $p=1,\dots,p_{\max}$ on a common sample.

```{r select}
sel <- var_select(yraw, pmax = 8)
sel$selection
```

AIC and FPE favour long lags, HQ and SC pick $p=2$. We take two lags as a
parsimonious baseline.

## 3. Estimation

```{r fit}
fit <- varm(y, p = 2)
fit
```

The tibble summaries are the quickest way to read a fit: `tidy()` is the
coefficient table (one row per equation and regressor), `glance()` the one-row
model summary and `augment()` the data with fitted values and residuals.

```{r tidy-fit}
co <- tidy(fit, conf.int = TRUE)
co[co$response == "rate", ]
glance(fit)
augment(fit)
```

`fit$B` is the $(Kp+d)\times K$ coefficient matrix (lags first, then constant;
one column per equation), `fit$Sigma` the residual covariance
(degrees-of-freedom corrected), `resid(fit)` the residuals, and `lag_matrices()`
the $K\times K\times p$ array of lag matrices.

```{r summary}
s <- summary(fit)
round(s$r.squared, 3)
round(lag_matrices(fit)[, , 1], 3)
```

`summary(fit)` prints the full equation-by-equation tables. Standard errors are
OLS standard errors with covariance $\hat\Sigma\otimes(X'X)^{-1}$. For Wald and
Granger tests and residual diagnostics (which start from `augment(fit)`), see
Sections 4-5 of `vignette("var-theory")`.

## 4. Stability

A VAR is stationary if all eigenvalues of the companion matrix lie inside the
unit circle. `stability()` returns their moduli.

```{r stability}
round(drop(stability(fit)), 3)
```

The largest modulus (0.95, also `max_root` in `glance(fit)`) is close to one: typical for macro levels, and a
reminder that long-horizon results are sensitive to small changes in persistence.

## 5. Impulse responses with bands

`irf()` defaults to a recursive (Cholesky) identification in the column order of
the data (`infl`, `unemp`, `rate`) and a residual bootstrap with 68% and 90%
bands. The rate is ordered last, so it is the "monetary policy" shock that
responds to inflation and unemployment on impact but does not affect them on
impact. Other identification schemes (long-run, sign restrictions, proxies,
heteroskedasticity) are in `vignette("identification")`, "Structural identification: from Cholesky to proxies and
sign restrictions". To choose a different order, use tidyselect:
`id_chol(order = c(rate, infl, unemp))`.

```{r irf}
ir <- irf(fit, horizon = 16, nboot = 500)      # bootstrap, Cholesky
ir
```

The point estimate is in `$estimate` (response x shock x horizon, horizon 0 =
impact), bands in `$bands` (response x shock x horizon x quantile), and `tidy()`
gives the same information as a tibble with columns `response`, `shock`, `horizon`,
`estimate` and, for each band, `level`, `conf.low` and `conf.high`. `normalise_to()`
rescales a shock, for example to a one percentage point rise in the rate, and
`cumulative` accumulates responses of variables entered in differences. Use
`ci = "wild"` if residual volatility changes over time (it does here: the Great
Moderation), `"mc"` for fast asymptotic bands, and `ci = "none"` for point estimates
only.

```{r irf-unit, fig.height = 3.4}
ir1 <- irf(fit, horizon = 16, ci = "wild", nboot = 500,
           normalise = normalise_to(rate, rate, 1))
autoplot(ir1, shocks = rate) +
  labs(title = "Responses to a 1pp policy-rate shock") +
  theme_varm()
```

`autoplot(ir)` draws a response-by-shock grid as a `ggplot2` object (rows:
responding variable, columns: shock) and takes tidyselect `shocks =` and
`responses =` arguments to subset. `plot(ir)` is a thin wrapper that prints the same
plot.

```{r plot, fig.height = 4}
autoplot(ir, shocks = rate)
```

The shaded areas are the 90% (light) and 68% (dark) pointwise bands: after a
policy-rate shock, the rate decays slowly (own-persistence of about 0.9 per
quarter), unemployment rises with a lag, and inflation moves little and with wide
uncertainty.

## 6. Forecast error variance decomposition

```{r fevd}
fv <- fevd(fit, horizon = 16, ci = "none")
round(fv$estimate[, , 17], 2)    # rows: variable, columns: shock, horizon 16
```

Each row sums to one. At horizon 16, about 80% of the forecast-error variance of
inflation comes from its own shock, whereas the rate is explained roughly 40% by
inflation shocks and 26% by unemployment shocks. Bands for FEVDs
(`fevd(fit)` with a bootstrap) are wide, since they are ratios of squared IRFs.

## 7. Historical decomposition

`hd()` splits the observed path into a baseline (deterministic part and initial
conditions) and the contributions of each structural shock. `autoplot()` stacks the
contributions as columns and draws the actual series as a line; `tidy()` returns the
long table (`time`, `response`, `shock`, `contribution`, `actual`).

```{r hd}
h <- hd(fit)
dim(h$contributions)             # time x variable x shock
max(abs(h$actual - h$baseline - apply(h$contributions, c(1, 2), sum)))   # exact identity
```

```{r hd-plot, fig.height = 3, warning = FALSE}
autoplot(h, responses = unemp)
```

## 8. Forecasts

`forecast()` iterates the VAR forward. The default bands are predictive: they
combine parameter draws (asymptotic Monte Carlo) with simulated future shocks.

```{r fc, fig.height = 3.4}
fc <- forecast(fit, h = 12, nboot = 500)
round(fc$mean[c(1, 4, 8, 12), ], 2)
```

```{r fc-plot, fig.height = 3.4}
autoplot(fc, n_history = 24)
```

## 9. A Bayesian VAR in three lines

`bvarm()` fits a conjugate Normal-inverse-Wishart VAR with a Minnesota prior
(shrinking towards a random walk in levels). The result plugs into the same
`irf()`, `fevd()`, `hd()` and `forecast()` generics, now with posterior bands. The
MCMC sizes below are deliberately small to keep this document fast; use thousands of
draws in practice.

```{r bvar}
b <- bvarm(y, p = 4, prior = prior_minnesota(), ndraw = 500, nburn = 200)
ib <- irf(b, horizon = 16)
round(ib$estimate[, "rate", c(1, 5, 9, 17)], 3)
```

```{r bvar-plot, fig.height = 3.4}
autoplot(ib, shocks = rate)
```

Hierarchical priors (`prior_minnesota(hyper = "full")`), stochastic volatility
(`bvarm(sv = TRUE)`), triangular samplers (`prior_triangular()`) and
are covered in `vignette("bayesian-var")`, "Bayesian VARs: priors, samplers and
diagnostics". Time-varying-parameter VARs (`tvpvar()`) are in `vignette("tvp-var")`,
"Time-varying-parameter VARs with stochastic volatility".

## 10. A local projection in three lines

`lp()` estimates the impulse response directly, with one regression per horizon
and Newey-West standard errors, with no dynamic model to get wrong.

```{r lp}
l <- lp(y, shock = rate, horizon = 16, lags = 2, contemp = c(infl, unemp))
round(l$estimate[c(1, 5, 9, 17), ], 3)     # horizon x response; a unit shock to the rate
```

`l$estimate` is a horizon-by-response matrix for a one-unit shock to `rate`, with
`l$bands` and `l$se` alongside. With `contemp` equal to the variables ordered before
the shock, this is the local-projection analogue of the Cholesky VAR response; compare
it with `irf(fit, normalise = normalise_to(rate, rate, 1))`. `autoplot(l)` plots the
projection and `tidy(l)` returns `horizon`, `response`, `estimate`, `std.error` and
band columns.

```{r lp-plot, fig.height = 3}
autoplot(l)
```

See `vignette("local-projections")`, "Local projections and the LP versus VAR
trade-off", for instrumental-variable LPs, simultaneous (sup-t) bands and the
comparison with VARs, and `vignette("lp-advanced")`, "Advanced local projections:
state dependence, smoothing, panels, joint inference and forecasting".

## 11. The tidy workflow

Everything above returns tibbles on request, so summaries and custom graphics need
no special tools. Two examples. First, a coefficient plot from `tidy(fit)` with
`ggplot2`, using the confidence limits that `conf.int = TRUE` adds:

```{r tidy-coef, fig.height = 3.6}
co <- co[co$term != "const", ]
ggplot(co, aes(estimate, term)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high), colour = varm_palette(1)) +
  facet_wrap(vars(response), labeller = label_both) +
  labs(x = "Coefficient (95% confidence interval)", y = NULL) +
  theme_varm()
```

Second, `tidy(irf)` into a hand-built plot. The bands are stacked in rows, one per
`level`; the point estimate repeats on each of them. Here we compare the wild
bootstrap (`ir1` above) with the asymptotic bands for the response of unemployment
to the 1pp rate shock, and summarise the peak response:

```{r tidy-irf, fig.height = 3}
ir_mc <- irf(fit, horizon = 16, ci = "mc", nboot = 500,
             normalise = normalise_to(rate, rate, 1))
both <- rbind(
  cbind(tidy(ir1), method = "wild bootstrap"),
  cbind(tidy(ir_mc), method = "mc")
)
u <- both[both$response == "unemp" & both$shock == "rate" & both$level == 0.9, ]
ggplot(u, aes(horizon, estimate)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high, fill = method), alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = varm_palette(2)) +
  labs(x = "Horizon (quarters)", y = "Unemployment response (pp)", fill = "90% band") +
  theme_varm()

# peak response and its horizon, from the same tibble
pk <- u[u$method == "wild bootstrap", ]
pk[which.max(pk$estimate), c("horizon", "estimate", "conf.low", "conf.high")]
```

The same pattern works for `tidy(fc)` (forecasts), `tidy(h)` (historical
decomposition), `tidy(l)` (local projections) and `tidy(b)` (Bayesian posterior
summaries); `glance()` gives one-row summaries (`glance(fit)`, `glance(b)`). The
outputs are plain tibbles, so base R (`aggregate()`, `split()`) and dplyr verbs work
on them directly.
